title: Why Did God Use an Imperfect Family?
paragraphs:
Why Did God Use an Imperfect Family?
The Scandal Hidden in Jesus' Family Tree Will Change How You See Your Own Story Forever
There is a question that quietly haunts countless hearts.
"If God already knows everything... why would He choose such broken people?"
It is the question of the divorced father who wonders if his failures have permanently disqualified him.
The single mother who carries shame that still whispers every night.
The child who grew up in a dysfunctional home.
The addict who believes heaven has closed its doors.
The believer who sincerely loves Jesus yet still wrestles with old wounds, hidden sins, painful memories, and a past that refuses to stay buried.
Perhaps it is your question too.
If God wanted to send the Savior of the world...
Why didn't He choose a perfect family?
Why not generations filled with flawless saints?
Why not a bloodline untouched by scandal?
Instead...
God did something that still shocks anyone willing to read the genealogy of Jesus carefully.
He intentionally preserved the names.
Every one of them.
Not to embarrass them.
But to reveal His glory.
Matthew begins his Gospel with words that many readers accidentally skip.

"Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ..."
(Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou.)
Literally,

"The book of the origin (or genealogy) of Jesus Christ."
(Matthew 1:1)
Matthew is announcing something much bigger than a family record.
He is announcing that a new creation has begun.
A new Genesis.
A new humanity.
A new King.
But before introducing the Savior...
God intentionally introduces the sinners.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
David.
Solomon.
The list keeps going.
Not one perfect man.
Not one perfect woman.
Not one spotless generation.
This is not an accident.
It is theology.
Because before Jesus saves sinners...
God wants you to know exactly who He came from.
Look closely.
Abraham lied.
Twice.
Out of fear, he called Sarah his sister (Genesis 12:10–20; 20:1–18).
Isaac repeated his father's deception (Genesis 26:6–11).

Jacob's very name, יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿaqov), is associated with grasping the heel and came to characterize him as one who supplants or deceives (Genesis 25:26; 27). Yet God later renamed him יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yiśrāʾēl), "Israel," after wrestling with him (Genesis 32:28). God did not deny Jacob's past; He transformed his future.
Judah slept with Tamar, believing she was a prostitute (Genesis 38).
King David committed adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrated the death of Uriah (2 Samuel 11).
Solomon, despite extraordinary wisdom, turned his heart toward the gods of his foreign wives (1 Kings 11).
The kingdom divided.
Kings rebelled.
Idolatry spread.
Exile followed.
The family line looked less like a royal success story and more like a long trail of human failure.
Yet through all of it...
God remained faithful to His covenant.
The Bible never celebrates these sins.
It records them truthfully so that God's mercy, not human goodness, becomes the center of the story.
Even more astonishing is that Matthew mentions women who would normally have been omitted from ancient Jewish genealogies.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
"The wife of Uriah."
Each name carries a story marked by pain, scandal, loss, or outsider status.
Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho who believed the God of Israel before many Israelites themselves showed faith (Joshua 2; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).
Ruth was a Moabite, a foreigner whose covenant loyalty brought her into God's redemptive plan (Ruth 1–4).
Bathsheba is not even named directly. Matthew simply writes, "the wife of Uriah," ensuring readers remember David's sin instead of allowing history to forget it (Matthew 1:6).
Why would God intentionally preserve these details?
Because grace shines brightest against the darkest background.
The Hebrew word often translated as steadfast love is חֶסֶד (ḥesed).
No single English word fully captures it.
It speaks of covenant love.
Faithful love.
Merciful loyalty.
Love that refuses to abandon.
Love that keeps pursuing.
Love rooted not in our worthiness but in God's own faithful character.
This is the heartbeat of Scripture.
God does not erase broken stories.
He redeems them.
When Joseph discovered Mary was pregnant, another scandal seemed ready to unfold.

Matthew says Joseph was "δίκαιος" (dikaios)—a righteous or just man (Matthew 1:19). His righteousness is seen not in harshness but in mercy. Before learning the divine origin of Mary's pregnancy, he intended to end the betrothal quietly rather than expose her to public disgrace.
Then an angel spoke.
"Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife..."
The child was conceived by the Holy Spirit.
And the angel declared:
"καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦν·"
"You shall call His name Jesus..."
"...for He will save His people from their sins."
(Matthew 1:21)
The Greek name Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous) corresponds to the Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua), meaning "Yahweh saves."
His very name announced His mission.
Not to seek perfect people.
But to save sinners.
The genealogy is not merely the family tree of Jesus.
It is a testimony that God keeps His promises through generations of imperfect people.
This does not excuse sin.

Scripture repeatedly calls people to repentance. David confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). Peter wept bitterly after denying Christ (Luke 22:62). Repentance is never minimized. Yet God's grace proves greater than the sins of those who truly turn to Him.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice...
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became respectable.
While we were still sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
Many people believe they must clean themselves before coming to Jesus.
The Gospel says the opposite.
Come to Jesus so He can cleanse you.
Some believe their family history defines their future.
The Gospel says Jesus creates a new family.
Some believe generational failures are stronger than God's promises.
The Gospel says Christ inaugurates a new covenant in His blood.
Some believe their shame is the loudest voice.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
If your family carries divorce...
Jesus is greater.
If your family carries addiction...
Jesus is greater.
If your family carries abuse...
Jesus is greater.
If your family carries unbelief...
Jesus is greater.
If your family carries secrets...
Jesus is greater.
If your own life carries regrets you cannot erase...
Jesus is still greater.
Because the central message of Scripture has never been that remarkable people found God.
It is that the holy God sought sinners through His Son.
That is why the genealogy matters.
Every broken branch eventually leads to the cross.
Every promise eventually points to Christ.
Every failure highlights humanity's need for a Savior.
Every page whispers the same hope:
Jesus came.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.

And everyone who repents and believes in Him receives forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life—not because of personal merit but because of God's grace through faith in Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Perhaps you have spent years believing your story is too damaged.
Too messy.
Too embarrassing.
Too far gone.
The genealogy of Jesus quietly answers you.
Look again.
God already knew every chapter before writing your invitation into His redemption story.
He never required a perfect family to accomplish His perfect plan.
He requires faith in His perfect Son.
Maybe today is the day you stop defining yourself by the worst chapter of your life.
Maybe today is the day you let Jesus become the Author of the next one.
Because the greatest miracle in the genealogy is not that broken people appear in it.
The greatest miracle is that the Holy One willingly stepped into it.
He entered our broken family so that everyone who trusts in Him could be adopted into His.

If this truth reached your heart, don't let it end with you. Whether it's "Jesus, rewrite my story," "Pray for me," or "Christ is still healing me," your testimony may become the encouragement another believer needs today.
Your past may explain your scars, but it never gets to author your eternity.
